configuration.content:
One of the things I wanted to achieve with my home server was to have a single place where I could store all my media, regardless of which physical drive the actual file resides on.

I hated how I needed to remember different mount points, different directories, and which drive has how much space left. Every time I want to store something, I had to think about where it should go.

I wanted some of my external drives merged in and be accessible through one folder: /data.

This is where mergerfs comes in.

mergerfs is a union filesystem that allows us to combine multiple filesystems and present them as a single directory. The interesting part is that it does this without actually merging the physical drives or changing how they store data. Each drive remains independent, and mergerfs simply provides a unified view of their contents.

This is particularly useful for a home server where you might have several drives of different capacities and want to make use of all of them without getting into a more complicated storage setup.

Let's set it up.

1. Install mergerfs

First, we need to install mergerfs. On Debian-based distributions, we can install it directly through APT.

sudo apt update
sudo apt install mergerfs

2. Identify the connected drives

Before doing anything with the drives, make sure there are no running processes accessing the directories or filesystems we're about to work with.

Next, identify the external drives connected to the server.

lsblk

This will list the available block devices along with their partitions, filesystem types, sizes, and mount points.

Identify the drives you want to include in the pool. For this setup, I'll refer to them as /dev/sdX1, /dev/sdX2, and /dev/sdX3. These are just examples, so make sure you replace them with the actual device identifiers on your system.

A small but important note: Device names such as /dev/sda and /dev/sdb are not guaranteed to remain the same across reboots or when devices are reconnected. We'll use filesystem UUIDs later to avoid depending on those names.

3. Format the drives (if necessary)

mergerfs doesn't require a particular filesystem, but I'll be using ext4 for these drives.

If the drives already have an ext4 filesystem and contain data you want to keep, you can skip this step.

Otherwise, format each drive:

sudo mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdX1
sudo mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdX2
sudo mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdX3

Be careful here. Formatting a drive will destroy its existing filesystem and can make its data inaccessible. Double-check the device identifiers before executing these commands.

4. Create mount points

Each physical drive needs its own mount point. These directories will serve as the individual branches of our storage pool.

I'll create them under /mnt.

sudo mkdir -p /mnt/disk1 /mnt/disk2 /mnt/disk3

We also need a directory where the combined filesystem will eventually be accessible.

sudo mkdir -p /data

This /data directory will be our final entry point. Instead of accessing each drive individually, we'll use this directory to access everything.

5. Mount the individual drives

Now, let's mount each drive to its respective mount point.

sudo mount /dev/sdX1 /mnt/disk1
sudo mount /dev/sdX2 /mnt/disk2
sudo mount /dev/sdX3 /mnt/disk3

At this point, all three drives should be accessible independently.

You can verify that by running:

lsblk

Or:

df -h

6. Get the UUIDs of the drives

We don't want to rely on device names when configuring automatic mounting. Instead, we'll use UUIDs.

Run:

sudo blkid

This will display the filesystem information for the connected drives, including their UUIDs.

Note down the UUID of each drive. We'll need these when configuring /etc/fstab.

7. Configure automatic mounting through fstab

Currently, the drives are mounted, but these mounts won't necessarily survive a reboot. We need to configure them to mount automatically.

Open the filesystem table:

sudo nano /etc/fstab

Add an entry for each drive:

UUID=<uuid-disk1> /mnt/disk1 ext4 defaults,noatime 0 2
UUID=<uuid-disk2> /mnt/disk2 ext4 defaults,noatime 0 2
UUID=<uuid-disk3> /mnt/disk3 ext4 defaults,noatime 0 2

Replace the placeholders with the actual UUIDs obtained earlier.

Here, noatime prevents the filesystem from updating access timestamps every time a file is read. It's a small optimization that can help reduce unnecessary writes.

Save the file and test the configuration:

sudo mount -a

If there are no errors, the entries should be configured correctly.

8. Merge the drives using mergerfs

Now comes the interesting part.

We have three independently mounted drives, each accessible through its own directory. Let's bring them together.

Run:

sudo mergerfs -o defaults,allow_other,use_ino,category.create=epmfs,statfs=full,minfreespace=1G \
/mnt/disk1:/mnt/disk2:/mnt/disk3 /data

That's it. The drives are now accessible through a single directory.

You can verify the mounted filesystem with:

df -h /data

And list its contents with:

ls -lah /data

A few words about the options we're using:

  • allow_other: Allows users other than the one mounting mergerfs to access the pooled filesystem, subject to the underlying filesystem permissions.

  • use_ino: Makes mergerfs provide inode information from the underlying filesystems.

  • category.create=epmfs: Determines where new files are created. It prefers a drive where the target directory already exists and, among those drives, chooses the one with the most available space. If no existing path is available, it falls back to the most-free-space policy.

  • statfs=full: Reports the combined filesystem capacity rather than limiting the reported size to a single branch.

  • minfreespace=1G: Prevents the creation policy from selecting a drive with less than 1 GB of available space.

  • defaults: Uses the default mount options.

9. Make the mergerfs pool persistent

The previous command mounts the pool for the current session. We also want it to be available automatically after every reboot.

For that, we'll add another entry to /etc/fstab.

Open it again:

sudo nano /etc/fstab

Add the following:

/mnt/disk1:/mnt/disk2:/mnt/disk3 /data fuse.mergerfs defaults,allow_other,use_ino,category.create=epmfs,statfs=full,minfreespace=1G,x-systemd.requires-mounts-for=/mnt/disk1,x-systemd.requires-mounts-for=/mnt/disk2,x-systemd.requires-mounts-for=/mnt/disk3 0 0

The x-systemd.requires-mounts-for options ensure that systemd mounts the individual drives before attempting to mount the mergerfs pool. This is important because we don't want the pool to be mounted against empty directories before the actual drives are ready.

Once you've saved the file, reload systemd's configuration and test the mounts:

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo mount -a

If everything works as expected, the storage pool should now be mounted automatically whenever the server boots.

10. Set the appropriate permissions

One last thing worth taking care of is permissions.

mergerfs doesn't override the permissions of the underlying filesystems. This means that even though everything is accessible through /data, the individual drives still retain their own ownership and permission settings.

If your intended user has UID and GID 1000, for example, you can assign ownership of the root directories of the individual drives:

sudo chown 1000:1000 /mnt/disk1 /mnt/disk2 /mnt/disk3

You can check your actual UID and GID using:

id

If the drives already contain files, remember that their existing permissions will still apply. You may need to adjust those separately depending on your requirements.

And we're done!

We now have multiple physical drives accessible through a single directory: /data.

The best part is that we haven't sacrificed the independence of the individual drives. We can still mount and access them separately whenever necessary. If one drive becomes unavailable, the data stored on the other drives remains accessible through their respective filesystems.

Of course, this isn't RAID, and it doesn't provide redundancy or data protection. If a drive fails, the data stored on that particular drive can still be lost. mergerfs is simply making multiple filesystems feel like one.

For my home server, that's exactly what I wanted: a simple way to expand storage capacity without having to worry about which physical drive I'm writing to every time I store something.

Thank you for reading. 🙏
